title: Ein Keloheinu
description: A Hebrew hymn of the Sabbath morning service, in the four-part setting the Union Hymnal printed in 1897, on Julius Freudenthal's tune. Its five short verses praise Hashem as our Master, our King and our Saviour: there is none like Hashem, who is like Hashem, we give thanks to Hashem, blessed is Hashem, and You are Hashem. Steady and bright, sung in Hebrew.

credits.arrangement: the Union Hymnal's four parts (1897), probably Julius Freudenthal's, adapted by Stackapella

licence.tune: public domain: Julius Freudenthal, first printed 1843; he died in 1874
licence.arrangement: the four voice parts the Union Hymnal printed in 1897, whose music it says was "selected and arranged by the Society of American Cantors", its index giving the source only as "German"; the 1932 edition credits the setting to Julius Freudenthal (died 1874), whose tune it is. Public domain either way: an anonymous work published in the US in 1897, out of copyright in the US (published before 1931) and in the EU and UK (the anonymous-work term, 70 years from publication, ended in 1967); and our parts already differ from the print in about a dozen places. Adapted for 2 to 4 beginners (bars and pitches as printed, in F): where the tune has the root or fifth, the alto takes the chord's third and the tenor the note it gave up (bar 1 and the fifth verse's first bar: alto A3 and tenor F3 on the first chord; bar 5 and its coda twin: alto A4 and F4, tenor C4; bar 6 and its twin: alto F4 under the tune's D5); no unison between tune and alto on 'cha' (bar 11), on the half close (bar 16, where the alto ends a third above the tune's low C) or on the last chord (alto a third above, tenor on the fifth); no doubled E (bars 9 and 13); the fifth verse's pickup, printed in bare octaves, sung as a C chord; under a slurred syllable each harmony part sings one note (bars 2, 13, 21; the coda's E-flat under 'mal' left out); breaths written in for beginners; the final fermata held two beats. Accepted exceptions (singable.py): the tune's own range as printed, its low C sharp on "shi-" a semitone under the beginner soprano range; where the tune ends on D at "nu." the alto sings F sharp, a third above it, so the duet ends with the chord's third.
licence.source: The Union Hymnal (text edited by the Central Conference of American Rabbis, music selected and arranged by the Society of American Cantors; Central Conference of American Rabbis, sold by Bloch Publishing Co., New York, copyright 1897; 1st edition), Appendix A (Hebrew Hymns and Responses), No. 17, "En Kelohenu", pp. 140 to 141, four voices on two staves, Andante con moto, in F, no composer on the page (index, p. 218: "German"); the tune is Julius Freudenthal's (1805 to 1874), first printed in Gesänge der Synagoge zu Braunschweig (1843), and the 1932 edition of the Union Hymnal credits him with the same setting. Written here in G, a tone up, so the tune (C-sharp 4 to E5 here) sits in the soprano's range. Printed with verses 1 and 3 under bars 1 to 8, verses 2 and 4 under bars 9 to 16 (verses 3 and 4 splitting the first half note of some bars), a D.S., then verse 5 ('Atto hu') with its own pickup; sung here in order, with a short rest before verse 5. The words are the print's, respelled from its Ashkenazi transliteration ('En kelohenu', 'Node', 'Boruch', 'Atto hu') in modern Israeli pronunciation (ch for the guttural, ' for a vowel the print elides), syllable for syllable as the notes carry them. Read from the scan at archive.org/details/unionhymnal0000unse_l7i5 (leaves n145 and n146); divine names in substituted forms (Hillel, 2026-11-11), the forms customary when singing outside prayer: Elokeinu, Kelokeinu, Chelokeinu, Lelokeinu, as the custom is (Adoneinu, not the Name, is kept).
